rv.q: And yet you never feel Rosalind and Celia’s closeness; the two stand at opposite ends of the stage as Celia declares “thou and I am one” after Rosalind’s banishment by Duke Frederick (Colm Gormley), but with a conspicuous sense of courtly performance that undercuts earnestness or intimacy.
Even if it doesn’t always convince emotionally, this pacy production, which leans into the play’s bawdy humour, is still rambunctious fun.
This now feels like a powerhouse team, simultaneously celebrating Shakespeare’s poetry and the contemporary stories they can tell with it.
This is Shakespearean comedy of the highest quality, very much as we like it and very much as you will like it too.
This crowd-pleasing As It continues the Globe's golden summer of productions.

A rollicking summer at Shakespeare’s Globe continues with this raucously entertaining take on As It, a surpassingly sweet play that seems here to take its cue from a passing reference near the end to “rustic revelry”.
This is Shakespearean comedy at its very best in a performance that throws the extraordinary language around with lighthearted revelry.

Lola Shalam’s take on Rosalind, perhaps Shakespeare’s most finely crafted female character, highlights her open pursuit of sexual desire, and hints at the gender euphoria the character might feel when dressing as Ganymede.

Ultimately, it was Lola Shalam’s night and rarely have I heard the throw away line “Do you not know I am a woman? When I think, I must speak.” delivered with such self-awareness and knowing parody of societal expectations.
All the World may be a Stage, but on this stage, this world was a disappointment.
If laughter and engagement shall be the measures of a comedy’s success, this one had both in spades.
This is a fun, fierce and fabulous production which will catapult the scorching heat of summer into your Autumn cosiness.
Hilarious and vibrant from start to finish, Holmes and Josephine's revival isn't simply theatre, but an event.
A delightfully witty yet accessible comedy which brings one of Shakespeare’s more verbose works to life.
This production of As It makes easy work of Shakespeare’s complex narrative full of disguises, misunderstandings, various degrees of exile, snobbery, and even a wrestling match.
This production feels similarly like a mashup of the best bits of other comedies.
It falls just short of being as successful as I would have liked.

cn.t: Critics find this energetic Globe production warm rather than rapturous, praising Lola Shalam's Rosalind and the company's fizzing performances, though some feel the Georgian court setting and directorial choices don't always convince emotionally.
